in_context.text: Jude says he had been eager to write about the salvation all believers share. But false teachers had slipped into the church, so he felt he must write instead to urge the readers to fight for the faith handed down to them once for all. The next verse gives the reason: ungodly men were turning God's grace into an excuse for sin and denying the Lord.

speaker.text: Jude, who calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. Tradition identifies him as the Judas named among Jesus' brothers.

audience.text: Believers he calls beloved: those sanctified by God the Father, preserved in Jesus Christ, and called. The letter does not say where they lived.

affected.text: The false teachers who had crept in unnoticed. They turned grace into lasciviousness, meaning shameless immorality, and denied the Lord.

what.text: Jude changes his writing plan from a general letter on shared salvation to an urgent appeal. He urges believers to contend earnestly for the faith delivered once for all to God's people.

events.text: The verse describes a time when false teachers had already entered the church. The text gives no date for this.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 65-80, by Jude the brother of James and of Jesus. Scholarly view: dates range from the 50s to the early second century, and some think a later follower wrote in Jude's name while others defend Jude's authorship.

where.text: Neither the place of writing nor the readers' location is stated. The letter's many references to Israel's history and Jewish tradition suggest readers who knew them well.

purpose.text: Jude wants believers to guard the faith they received against men who were twisting grace into license and denying Christ.

big_picture.text: This verse states the theme of the whole letter. Jude then gives examples of God's judgment (1:5-16) and ends by calling readers to build themselves up in their most holy faith and keep themselves in God's love (1:20-21).

for_readers.text: Other Scripture also calls believers to stand for the faith. Paul urges 'striving together for the faith of the gospel' (Philippians 1:27) and says, 'I have kept the faith' (2 Timothy 4:7).

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted to justify harsh, combative arguing with anyone who disagrees on any religious point.

in_context_reading.text: Jude's target is men who turned grace into immorality and denied the Lord (1:4). In the same letter he notes that Michael did not bring a railing accusation against the devil (1:9). He also tells readers to show compassion and rescue others (1:22-23), so contending means guarding the core faith, not quarrelsome harshness.

why_it_matters.text: The lexicon defines it as to contend with, or to contend for, and lists Jude 3 for the sense 'contend for' a thing. Here the thing fought for is the faith.
In this verse the lexicon gives the sense 'once for all,' as in Hebrews 9:28 and 1 Peter 3:18. The faith was delivered fully, not in ongoing new installments.
It means to give or hand over to another. Romans 6:17 uses it of being delivered up to a course of teaching, which pictures the faith as something passed on.
Here it means common in the sense of shared or general, not ordinary or unclean. The lexicon groups it with Titus 1:4, 'the common faith.'

takeaway.text: Jude calls believers to guard the shared faith they received once for all, especially against teaching that excuses sin. In the same letter he pairs that firmness with prayer, God's love and compassion.
